nameStory: The name 'dandelion' comes from the French 'dent de lion,' meaning 'lion's tooth,' referring to the deeply jagged edges of the leaves that look like fierce lion fangs. Some folks also call the fluffy seed heads 'blowballs' or 'clocks' because children traditionally blow on them to tell time or make wishes.
description: The common dandelion is a low-growing perennial herb that forms flat rosettes of deeply toothed leaves spreading 6-12 inches across. It produces bright yellow flower heads on hollow stems that can reach 2-18 inches tall, followed by the familiar white, globe-shaped seed heads that kids love to blow apart. This hardy plant can pop up almost anywhere, from sidewalk cracks to pristine lawns, and blooms from early spring through late fall.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves grow in a flat rosette from the base with no stem leaves, featuring deep, jagged teeth pointing backward toward the center (like lion's teeth). They feel smooth and slightly waxy, often with a bitter, milky sap when broken.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flower heads made up of many tiny ray petals (no center disc), sitting alone atop hollow, smooth stems. The flowers close up at night and on cloudy days, opening wide in sunny weather.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Transforms into a perfect white globe of seeds, each topped with a feathery parachute (pappus) that feels silky to touch. These 'blowballs' are unmistakable and irresistible to blow apart.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, flat rosettes that hug the ground, with flower stems rising directly from the center. Stems are completely hollow - you can blow through them like straws and they contain bitter, white milky sap.

habitat: Dandelions thrive virtually everywhere in New England - lawns, roadsides, fields, gardens, waste areas, and even sidewalk cracks. They prefer moist, fertile soils but tolerate poor, compacted earth and can handle both full sun and partial shade. You'll find them from sea level to mountain meadows, often dominating disturbed areas.

seasonality.spring: First flowers appear in early spring (March-April), providing crucial early nectar for emerging bees and other pollinators. New leaf rosettes emerge bright green and tender.
seasonality.summer: Continuous cycle of flowering and seed production throughout summer, with plants producing multiple generations. Leaves become tougher and more bitter in heat.
seasonality.fall: Still blooming and setting seed into late fall, often producing a second flush of tender leaves. Seeds continue dispersing on autumn breezes.
seasonality.winter: Leaves may persist in mild winters as a low rosette, though they often die back to the deep taproot. Look for dried, hollow stems and lingering seed heads.

funFact: A single dandelion plant can produce over 2,000 seeds per year, and each seed can travel over 60 miles on the wind thanks to their perfectly engineered parachute design that inspired the creation of parachutes for humans!
confusionNotes: Young dandelion rosettes might be confused with other 'weedy' plants like plantain or chicory, but dandelions are the only ones with those distinctive backward-pointing leaf teeth and hollow flower stems. Memory trick: 'Lion's teeth bite backward toward the den (center of the rosette).'
contextualKnowledge: Though often despised as a lawn weed, dandelions are actually non-native plants from Europe that have become so established they're practically honorary natives. Every part is edible - young leaves for salads, flowers for wine, and roots for coffee substitute - and they're packed with vitamins A, C, and K.
compareHints: Common dandelion is much more widespread than its relatives in New England. Red-seeded dandelion has similar flowers but produces reddish seeds instead of white ones. The key difference from other yellow composite flowers is dandelion's combination of deeply toothed basal leaves, hollow stems, and the lack of any center disc in the flower head.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red-seeded dandelion is most easily distinguished from common dandelion by its reddish seeds rather than pale yellow ones.
Fen dandelion differs from common dandelion primarily in its exclusive wetland habitat and potentially smaller, more delicate features.
Among New England dandelions, only the cinnamon-fruited dandelion has distinctly brown seeds - common dandelion and red-seeded dandelion both have much paler, straw-colored to light brown fruits.
